{{Short description|Sequence of numbers}}
The '''Katydid sequence''' is a [[integer sequence|sequence]] of numbers first defined in [[Clifford A. Pickover]]'s book ''Wonders of Numbers'' (2001).

==Description==

A Katydid sequence is the smallest sequence of integers that can be reached from 1 by a sequence of the two operations ''n''&nbsp;↦&nbsp;2''n''&nbsp;+&nbsp;2 and 7''n''&nbsp;+&nbsp;7 (in any order).<ref name=cp>{{cite book|title=Wonders of Numbers: Adventures in Mathematics, Mind, and Meaning|first=Clifford A.|last=Pickover|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=2001|isbn=9780195348002|page=330|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=52N0JJBspM0C&pg=PA330}}</ref> For instance, applying the first operation to 1 produces the number 4, and applying the second operation to 4 produces the number 35, both of which are in the sequence.

The first 10 elements of the sequence are:<ref>{{Cite OEIS|A060031|name=Katydid sequence: closed under n -> 2n + 2 and 7n + 7}}</ref>
:1, 4, 10, 14, 22, 30, 35, 46, 62, 72.

==Repetitions==

Pickover asked whether there exist numbers that can be reached by more than one sequence of operations.<ref name=cp/>
The answer is yes. For instance, 1814526 can be reached by the two sequences
'''1, 4, 10, 22, 46, 329, 660, 4627, 9256, 18514, 37030, 259217, 1814526''' and
'''1, 14, 30, 62, 441, 884, 1770, 3542, 7086, 14174, 28350, 56702, 113406, 226814, 453630, 907262, 1814526'''.
